Heteropolyacids (HPAs) are early transition metal oxygen anion clusters (polyoxometalates) with well-defined molecular structures and tunable redox properties, which makes them useful as acid and oxidation catalysts and as model metal oxide molecules. The Keggin structure, for example \[PW12O40\]3-, has a central heteroatom tetrahedron surrounded by twelve WO6 octahedra, each carrying an outward-pointing terminal oxo group. The Wells-Dawson structure, for example \[P2W18O62\]6-, is an ellipsoidal anion built from two defect-Keggin fragments. On graphite, HPAs form ordered two-dimensional arrays, and their tunneling spectra show negative differential resistance at voltages that correlate with their reduction potentials. Related: [Scanning tunneling microscopy](/papers/topics/scanning-tunneling-microscopy/), [Negative differential resistance](/papers/topics/negative-differential-resistance/).

## HPA molecules as STM tip modifiers (2002)

Song, Kitchin and Barteau used H3PW12O40 (about 11 to 12 Å across, twelve terminal W=O groups) to functionalize Pt/Ir STM tips. The rigid structure was proposed to present a single terminal oxygen as an atomically sharp, stable apex, giving atomic resolution of graphite and molecular resolution of H6P2W18O62 monolayers (primitive cell 14.6 Å, 35.2°). Because the NDR voltage depends on HPA structure and composition, the authors suggest HPAs as a tunable family of tip functionalization agents, extending the C60 approach to semiconducting oxides ([Song et al. 2002](/papers/song2002/)). Summary: [song2002](/papers/song2002/).
